outline.description: Introduces the core concepts of tabular data, traditional supervised learning paradigms, and challenges that arise in low‑shot settings. The chapter lays the groundwork for understanding why recent advances in LLMs are relevant for tabular problems.
subtopics: 1.1 Definition and Structure of Tabular Data
1.2 Conventional Learning Algorithms (LogReg, XGBoost, Random Forest)
1.3 Limitations of Small‑Sample Regimes
1.4 Early Few‑Shot Techniques (bootstrapping, semi‑supervised, transfer learning)

outline.chapter_title: 2. Large Language Models: Beyond Natural Language
outline.description: Provides a concise overview of the evolution of LLMs, their pre‑training objectives, and how their internal knowledge can be leveraged beyond text tasks. Sets the stage for the subsequent discussion on tokenizing tabular data as language.
subtopics: 2.1 From RNNs to Transformers and GPT‑style Models
2.2 Knowledge Representation in LLMs
2.3 Prior Works on LLMs for Structured Data (Lift, AnyPredict, TabLLM)
2.4 Practical Constraints: API access, prompt limits, computational cost

outline.chapter_title: 3. The Idea of Feature Engineering with LLMs
outline.description: Explains the conceptual shift from end‑to‑end prediction to feature generation via rule extraction. Discusses how human experts traditionally engineer features and how LLMs can emulate this process through few‑shot prompting.
subtopics: 3.1 Human Feature Engineering vs Algorithmic Feature Engineering
3.2 Rules as Binary Features: Motivation and Benefits
3.3 Leveraging Prior Knowledge for Causal Inference in Tables
3.4 Advantages: Reduced latency, no per‑sample inference

outline.description: Presents the high‑level flow of FeatLLM: from data preparation to rule extraction, parsing, weight learning, and ensemble prediction.
subtopics: 4.1 Problem Formalization (Dataset notation, k‑shot setup)
4.2 End‑to‑End Pipeline Diagram
4.3 Key Design Choices (fixed 10 rules per class, bagging)

outline.description: Details the structured prompt design that guides an LLM to identify causal relationships and produce clean rule outputs suitable for parsing.
subtopics: 5.1 Basic Information Description - Task framing and feature metadata
5.2 Reasoning Instruction - Two‑stage reasoning protocol (prior knowledge + data example inference)
5.3 Response Instruction - Standardized output formatting for rules and classes
5.4 Practical Tips: Managing token limits, temperature tuning

outline.chapter_title: 6. From Natural Language Rules to Binary Features
outline.description: Describes how the model transforms LLM–generated natural language rules into executable code that evaluates each sample against all rules.
subtopics: 6.1 Challenges of Noisy NLP Output (verbal vs symbolic operators)
6.2 Co‐prompting an LLM for Parsing Code Generation
6.3 Executing Generated Code with Python exec() and Safety Considerations
6.4 Example Walkthrough

outline.chapter_title: 7. Learning Rule Importance with a Linear Classifier
outline.description: Explains how a simple non‑negative linear model is trained on the binary rule features to obtain class logits and probabilities.
subtopics: 7.1 Feature Vector Construction (z_k^i per class)
7.2 Weight Projection to Non‑Negative Space (max(·,0))
7.3 Softmax Likelihood Estimation
7.4 Cross‑Entropy Optimization and Hyperparameters

outline.description: Illustrates how repeated sampling of training data or features coupled with high‐temperature prompting introduces diversity; ensemble predictions improve robustness especially under large feature sets.
subtopics: 8.1 Randomization Sources (temperature, demo order)
8.2 Feature Bagging vs Instance Bagging
